title: Engineering kekule superconductivity from layer-selective interactions in rhombohedral graphene
abstract: At weak coupling, finite-momentum superconductivity is typically associated with broken time-reversal or inversion symmetry of the Fermi surface. Here, we show that lattice-scale pair-density-wave order in rhombohedral multilayer graphene can arise from layer/orbital-dependent pairing interactions, band chirality, and Dirac-point-centered Fermi surface topology while preserving both symmetries. Using mean-field theory and comparing finite momentum sectors $Q = \pm 2 K_{D}$ with the $ Q = 0$ superconducting state, we find that layer-dependent interactions of opposite signs ($V_{1A}=-V_{JB}=-|V|$) favor an intra-valley Kekulè state with center-of-mass momentum ($ Q=\pm 2 K_D$). In the presence of a time-reversal and inversion symmetry-preserving Kane-Mele mass ($λ$), this state appears only above a critical carrier density ($n^{crit}_{K}(λ,J)$). The two superconducting condensates exhibit opposite chirality, $J(-J)$ for $K_D(-K_D) $ valleys, thereby preserving time-reversal and inversion symmetry. We map the phase diagram and analyze the dependence of $T_c$ on the chirality index $J$ and $λ$. We also evaluate the superfluid stiffness in the Kekulè superconducting state, thereby determining the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition temperature. Our results show that orbital-dependent interactions in the presence of band chirality favor finite-momentum pairing in time-reversal and inversion symmetric Dirac materials.
summary: This theoretical study demonstrates that in rhombohedral graphene, specific layer-dependent pairing interactions can stabilize a finite-momentum Kekulé superconducting state. By analyzing the competition between different pairing channels using mean-field theory, the authors show that this state can emerge while maintaining crucial symmetries like time-reversal and inversion symmetry. This work highlights the role of orbital structure and band chirality in engineering unconventional superconductivity.
main_problem: The paper addresses the mechanism for realizing finite-momentum superconductivity (Pair-Density-Wave, PDW) in a manner that preserves both time-reversal and inversion symmetries.
main_result: Orbital-dependent interactions in the presence of band chirality favor the formation of a Kekulé superconducting state with finite center-of-mass momentum, even in time-reversal and inversion symmetric Dirac materials.
method: The study employs mean-field theory applied to the pairing problem, comparing the superconducting instabilities in the zero-momentum ($Q=0$) and finite-momentum ($Q=\pm 2K_D$) sectors.
model_or_system: The system is rhombohedral multilayer graphene (RMG) described by an extended chiral Kane-Mele Hamiltonian. The analysis focuses on how layer/orbital-dependent pairing interactions drive the superconducting instability.
key_observables: Superconducting order parameters ($\Delta_{Q=0}$ vs $\Delta_{Q=\pm 2KD}$), superfluid stiffness, and the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition temperature ($T_{BKT}$).
important_parameters: Layer-dependent interaction signs ($V_{1A} = -V_{JB}$), the Kane-Mele mass term ($\lambda$), and the critical carrier density ($n_{crit}^K$).
main_assumptions: The analysis primarily uses onsite interactions and initially neglects remote-hopping effects, though later notes suggest layer-dependent renormalization effects can relax this assumption.
figures_summary: The notes reference schematics illustrating the competition between $Q=0$ (inter-valley) and $Q=\pm 2KD$ (intra-valley) Cooper-pair scattering processes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the theoretical framework using the Kane-Mele model, then analyzing the pairing instabilities in different momentum sectors using mean-field theory, and finally mapping the phase diagram to show the conditions favoring the finite-momentum Kekulé state.
why_interesting: The work provides a concrete, symmetry-preserving mechanism for unconventional superconductivity in a tunable 2D material, which is highly relevant for designing novel quantum electronic devices.
